lesson.title: Drawing an Atom by Its Valence Electrons Alone
lesson.summary: A Lewis dot symbol represents an element's chemical symbol surrounded by dots for each of its valence electrons, giving a quick visual shorthand for how many electrons an atom has available for bonding.
lesson.body:
Chemists rarely need to draw every electron in an atom to understand how it will bond. Core electrons, the ones packed into completely filled inner shells, are shielded from other atoms and essentially never participate in bonding. What matters for chemical behavior is the valence electrons, the electrons in the outermost occupied shell, and a Lewis dot symbol is simply a shorthand that shows exactly those electrons and nothing else: the element's chemical symbol, standing in for the nucleus and all core electrons together, surrounded by one dot for each valence electron.

The convention for placing the dots follows a simple pattern that mirrors how orbitals actually fill. Imagine the four sides of the element's symbol as four available positions. The first four valence electrons go one to a side, spread out as far as possible, and only once all four sides have one dot does a fifth electron begin pairing up with an existing one, continuing around until all four sides hold a pair. This ordering is not arbitrary bookkeeping, it reflects the real physical tendency of electrons to occupy separate orbitals before pairing up in the same one, the same principle that governs how p orbitals fill during electron configuration.

The number of valence electrons, and therefore the number of dots, connects directly to an element's group number for the main group elements. Sodium, in group 1, has one valence electron and gets a symbol with a single dot. Magnesium, group 2, gets two dots. Aluminum, group 13, gets three. Carbon, group 14, gets four dots, one on each side, none paired yet. Nitrogen, group 15, gets five: four sides each with one dot, plus one side now holding a second, paired dot. Oxygen, group 16, gets six: two sides paired, two sides still single. Fluorine, group 17, gets seven: three sides paired, one side single. Neon, group 18, gets a full eight, all four sides paired, the hallmark of a stable noble gas configuration that nothing else in that period can match.

This is exactly why elements in the same group share such similar chemical behavior: same number of valence electrons means the same Lewis dot symbol pattern, which means a similar number of electrons to gain, lose, or share to reach a stable configuration. Sodium and potassium, both group 1 with a single dot, both readily lose that one electron to form 1+ cations. Oxygen and sulfur, both group 16 with six dots, both tend to gain two electrons, or share two bonding pairs, to fill out to eight.

Lewis dot symbols become genuinely useful once two or more atoms are drawn together and their dots start to combine into shared pairs. A single atom's dot symbol shows what it has available to offer; connecting several atoms' dot symbols into a shared structure, complete with bonding pairs and leftover lone pairs, is exactly the subject of Lewis structures, the next step beyond representing one isolated atom.
